# The Only SaaS Moats Left in 2026

**Source:** [YouTube by Rob Walling](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KpILHX2D-AA) | Oct 18, 2026  
**Format:** Conference talk + framework  
**Duration:** 39:50 (auto-generated captions, 7,710 words)  
**Channel:** MicroConf (SaaS founder conference)
**Context:** Comprehensive analysis of which competitive moats survive in an AI-commoditized SaaS market

---

## Executive Summary

Rob Walling (MicroConf founder, SaaS Playbook author) + Interval Set analyze which business defensibility mechanisms still work when AI makes feature-building nearly free and competitors can reach feature parity in weeks.

**Thesis:** 10-20% of SaaS companies will decline or go to zero. The others survive by building one of **8 modern moats** that AI cannot quickly replicate.

**The bad news:** Most classic moats (unique features, owned traffic, clever code, UX familiarity, integrations, high switching costs) are degraded or eliminated by AI.

**The good news:** 8 new/evolved moats remain defensible. Companies with even 1-2 of these moats will survive and thrive.

---

## The 10 AI Attacks on SaaS

### Supply-Side Attacks (6)

When AI makes building features easy and cheap, supply increases → commoditization → price collapse.

**Attack 1: Customers build it themselves**
- AI makes it easy for non-technical users to build their own versions
- "They don't need your 50 features; they only need the 3 they use"
- AI coding assistants reduce the expertise barrier

**Attack 2: Competitors reach feature parity instantly**
- Example: 46+ AI note-takers exist (Otter, Fireflies, Krisp, Fathom, TLDR, Granola, etc.)
- Feature parity achievable in "a few months" with AI coding
- Features used to buy founders years of runway; now it buys weeks

**Attack 3: Open-source accelerates**
- Non-technical buyers can now deploy open-source (via Claude Code, talking to Claude)
- Open-source projects move faster with AI assistance
- High-quality free alternatives available

**Attack 4: Platform ships your feature for free**
- Platform providers (Salesforce, HubSpot, CRM systems, etc.) can build add-ons in weeks
- They already own the customer relationship
- Your UI is basically a spec for them to build off
- Example: CRM platforms integrating ancillary functions you sell as standalone tools

**Attack 5: Custom software at SaaS prices**
- Agencies used to charge $30-50k for 3-month builds
- With AI coding, they build in 1/3 to 1/5 the time
- Agencies now offer recurring ($299-999/month) custom solutions vs. your one-size-fits-all SaaS
- More defensible business model than pure SaaS

**Attack 6: LLMs absorb your product**
- Examples: Ad copy generation, headline generation, image generation tools → now built into LLMs
- Some product categories disappear as their function gets absorbed into general-purpose AI

### Demand-Side Attacks (4)

When AI disrupts your customers' businesses, they either reduce spending or disappear.

**Attack 7: Customer industries are decimated**
- Example: Transcription agencies, translation agencies → volume up but revenue down (AI is cheaper)
- Example: Copywriting services → disrupted by AI
- 80-90% of these customer segments go to zero, not 10-20%
- Result: Involuntary churn; no recovery path

**Attack 8: Seats collapse**
- Customer support: 8 human agents → 1-2 AI agents + supervisors
- Help desk software (Zendesk, Help Scout) faces massive seat contraction
- Companies moving to outcome-based pricing to adapt

**Attack 9: The thing you manage becomes obsolete**
- Example: Software for managing take-home coding tests → irrelevant (candidates use AI to solve them)
- Example: Software for hiring-interview workflows → changes if the hiring process changes

**Attack 10: Humans doing the work disappear**
- Receptionists, call center agents → replaced by AI agents
- If your software is for the human doing the work, you need to agentify or die
- "If you don't agentify your software, I think you're going to zero in the next couple years"
- Example: $50/month receptionist software vs. $300-500/month for AI agent doing the work

### Severity

**Rob's estimate:** 10-20% of SaaS companies will decline or go to zero in the next 2-3 years.

**Status:** Not all are equal threats. No single attack causes apocalypse, but 10 together create a problem.

---

## The 9 Classic SaaS Moats (Mostly Degraded)

These used to work. AI has weakened or eliminated most:

1. **Unique features** → AI makes features trivial to copy
2. **Strong brand** → Still works, but less effective alone
3. **Owned traffic channels (SEO)** → AI is trivializing marketing (50/50 on this one)
4. **Clever code / complex algorithms** → AI is solving historically-hard problems (100 math proofs solved)
5. **UX familiarity** → Irrelevant if systems go agentic (agents don't care about UI)
6. **Complex integrations** → APIs become specs for AI to code against
7. **High switching costs (data export friction)** → AI can extract data even without export buttons
8. **Multi-person coordination** → Still somewhat relevant
9. **System of record** → Still a moat (see updated moats below)

**Casualties:** Most of these are now 1-3 on a 0-100 scale. Only items 8-9 remain strong at 50+.

---

## The 8 Surviving Moats (2026+)

### Moat 1: Buyers Know and Trust You
**Definition:** Strong brand + established buyer relationships + partner ecosystem + champions inside customers

**Why it works:** Competitors with better code still must build all of this from zero.

**Traits:**
- Strong brand recognition in your market
- You know how your buyers buy (and they know you)
- Partners built their businesses recommending you
- Champions inside customer organizations will fight for you

**Examples:**
- **QuickBooks** — Every accountant uses it. "QuickBooks is terrible software, I hate using it, but my accountant uses it and he likes it." Better products lose.
- **Shopify** — Thousands of agencies implement Shopify stores. Merchants hire agencies → agencies → Shopify. Platform pre-decided.

**Evaluation question:** Who's built their business or career around recommending or defending you?

**Strength:** 8-9/10. Extremely hard to displace even with better technology.

---

### Moat 2: You Are a System of Record
**Definition:** The definitive source of truth for business data. Daily operations built around you. Can't be easily exported or migrated.

**Why it works:** Gravity. Once everything is wired in, switching is painful.

**Traits:**
- People log in every day to do work
- You're the operating system of that business (if you go down, business halts)
- Balances, approvals, statuses, workflows all configured in you
- Audit trails, roles, rules, integrations reading from you or writing to you
- Data doesn't cleanly come out

**Examples:**
- **Jira** — Developers, managers, product people, multiple teams all coordinated. Could export tickets in an afternoon, but migrating history, audit trail, integrations across teams would be "very, very painful."
- **GymDesk** (Tiny Seed) — Entire gym operations run on it. Started as one feature, expanded into invoicing, billing, hardware integration (RFID fobs). Massive switching cost.

**Evaluation question:** If your customer wants to leave, what can't they export? What breaks downstream? What would they have to rebuild?

**Strength:** 8-9/10. Gravity + operational lock-in is incredibly defensible.

---

### Moat 3: You're Allowed to Act
**Definition:** Your software doesn't just advise or report; it actually moves money, takes action, changes state.

**Why it works:** Action is irreversible and creates liability. Much harder to replicate than reporting.

**Traits:**
- You move money, not just recommend it
- You execute workflows, not just report on them
- You step into front of customer workflows and take action
- You don't just advise; you act

**Comparison:**
- Reporting tool: "Here's a list of people to pay with amounts"
- Action tool: "I'm moving the money to Venmo/PayPal for you"

**Examples:**
- **Stripe Connect** — Moves actual money. No one switches off Stripe Connect.
- **Reimbi** (Tiny Seed) — Reimbursement tool that pays candidates/contractors directly via Venmo, PayPal, Cash App. Handles all KYC/compliance automatically.
- **Churnkey** — Sits in cancellation flow, makes offers on your behalf to reduce churn. You don't even check if the offer was accepted.

**Evaluation question:** Can your software act, or can it only advise? Are you a reporting tool or something that actually does something?

**Strength:** 7-8/10. Action creates irreversibility and switching cost.

---

### Moat 4: Customers Trust Your Output Enough They Don't Check It
**Definition:** You've earned permission to be the source of truth. Customers don't verify your work.

**Why it works:** Verification would require understanding the domain deeply. Customers don't have time or expertise.

**Traits:**
- Customers trust you with critical decisions/data
- They don't verify the output
- You've been right for years, so they don't second-guess
- Breaking their trust means serious consequences for them

**Examples:**
- **Gusto** — Used since 2013. "I have never once checked their work. I could go to jail for IRS stuff if Gusto decided to mess me." Zero verification. Switching means hiring an accountant to audit everything.
- **Avalara** — Sales tax compliance tool. "We don't check the number. They've earned this permission."

**Evaluation question:** Do customers trust your output enough that they don't check you?

**Strength:** 8-9/10. Trust + regulatory risk make this incredibly defensible.

---

### Moat 5: Someone Official Already Said Yes
**Definition:** Regulatory approvals, certifications, licenses, accreditations that took years to earn and a competitor must re-earn.

**Why it works:** Regulatory walls are hard. Even if code is cheap, compliance is expensive and time-consuming.

**Traits:**
- You hold compliance certifications (SOC 2, HIPAA, ISO 27001, GDPR readiness, etc.)
- You hold industry-specific approvals (ABA board approval, SMS carrier registration, etc.)
- Competitor must earn the same approvals (expensive, time-consuming)
- These are speed bumps, not perfect walls, but they matter

**Examples:**
- **Compliance** — Vanta ($1B company) was founded to help with SOC 2/compliance. SOC 2 alone takes months and is brutally expensive. That's a moat.
- **ABA course platform** (Tiny Seed) — Courses count toward psychology credentials. Competitor must get board approval. That's a major barrier.
- **SMS compliance** — US SMS is shockingly hard. Carrier registration, consent laws, regulations. More moat than the software.

**Evaluation question:** What approvals, complexity, or legal stuff have you navigated that a competitor would have to earn?

**Strength:** 7-8/10. Regulatory walls are hard to cross but can be done.

---

### Moat 6: Everyone's Already in the Software (Network Effects)
**Definition:** Switching requires moving everyone at once. Coordination cost is high.

**Why it works:** Individuals can't leave; the whole group must move together. That's painful.

**Traits:**
- Multiple team members use your software
- Switching requires organization-wide agreement
- One person leaving isn't enough (the rest stay)
- Coordination cost is high
- Works better when users are non-technical

**Examples:**
- **Slack** — Prototypical network effect. Everyone tries to leave, no one does.
- **Commit Swimming** (Tiny Seed) — Swim team management. Get all the parents, coaches, swimmers into the platform. Switching means coordinating dozens of families + entire league. Pain threshold is very high.

**Evaluation question:** Would a competitor have to move everyone at once?

**Strength:** 8-9/10. Coordination cost creates defensibility even if the product is mediocre.

---

### Moat 7: Every Customer Makes Your Software Smarter (Learning Loops)
**Definition:** Data from one customer improves the product for all customers. Switching means losing access to this collective intelligence.

**Why it works:** Single customer can't replicate the intelligence. It requires network data. Switching loses the moat.

**Traits:**
- Every customer action improves the system for everyone
- Data is not siloed; it benefits all customers
- Customers can take their data but not what you learned from it
- System keeps learning over time (not stagnant)
- Competitors start from zero; you have years of data advantage

**Mechanics:**
1. Situation occurs (fraud, spam, miscategorization, etc.)
2. Human or software takes action
3. You observe the result
4. System corrects and improves
5. Improvement benefits all customers

**Examples:**
- **Stripe Radar** — Fraud detection. Every merchant sees fraud patterns, feeds up into collective intelligence. Individual merchant's data is worth way less than full Stripe Radar. Switching = losing the collective intelligence.
- **Ramp** — Bookkeeping. Every correction a customer makes ("This Verizon line is cell phone not internet") benefits all customers. Learning loops for expense categorization.
- **Mailchimp** — Spam detection engine (Omnivore). Learned spam patterns since 2009 (before modern AI). Collective intelligence is the moat.
- **Churnkey** — In theory, every churn offer + result should improve the model for all companies. (Rob hasn't verified if they're actually doing this)

**3-part gate (all must be true):**
1. Every customer makes it better for every other (not siloed)
2. Customers can export data but not what you learned from it
3. You keep learning (system improves over time)

**Evaluation question:** Does what happens to one customer make your product smarter for the rest?

**Strength:** 8-9/10. Data advantage compounds and is very hard to replicate.

---

### Moat 8: It's Hard to Keep Running
**Definition:** The software is not hard to build, but it's a pain to operate. The operational burden is the moat.

**Why it works:** Smart engineers avoid operational nightmares. The burden itself becomes defensible.

**Traits:**
- Build complexity is low (AI can handle this)
- Operational complexity is high (DevOps, infrastructure, maintenance, scaling)
- Someone has to babysit it forever
- Most people don't want the job

**Examples:**
- **ScrapingBee** — Web scraping isn't hard to build. But keeping it working + not getting blocked is "a pain in the ass." Requires cycling IPs, dealing with carrier registrations, proxies, etc. Peter Levels (indie hacker at extreme end of vibing everything) tried to clone it, gave up, pays $99/month. Eight-figure exit.
- **CloudFlare** — Same moat. Not hard to build, incredibly hard to keep running. Are you going to vibeCode CloudFlare and maintain it? No.
- **Drip** (ESP, RIP) — "Anyone can send an email." But fighting spam requires full-time people. Hooking into AWS SES is trivial; fighting the resulting abuse is a nightmare. Drip had multiple full-time employees whose only job was fighting spam.

**Evaluation question:** Is it hard to build or hard to keep running? Because the thing you hate and resent maintaining can actually be a moat.

**Strength:** 7-8/10. Operational burden deters competitors, but someone will eventually take it on.

## Market-Level Signal: Atlassian vs. HubSpot

In August 2026, both reported earnings. Same day, opposite outcomes:

**HubSpot:**
- Beat earnings, beat expectations
- $1B stock buyback announced
- Stock dropped 21%
- Reason: Their inbound marketing moat is "massively negatively impacted" by AI. Marketing is being commoditized.

**Atlassian:**
- Similar earnings results
- MCP server usage doubled
- AI was making the product better (learning loop)
- Stock up 35%
- Reason: Jira has multiple strong moats (system of record, learning loops via AI integration)

**Signal:** Tens of billions in market cap moving based on whether you have defensible moats against AI disruption.

---

## Why Moats Matter (Beyond Founders)

### For Private Equity / M&A

Private equity does 70% of SaaS acquisitions. They've historically paid high multiples (3-5x revenue) based on assumed growth.

**New dynamic:** PE buyers are terrified. Not about present performance, but about whether you'll exist in 3-5 years.

**Their buying criteria:** Does this company have defensible moats against AI? If yes, pay multiples. If no, deep discount or pass.

**A&R's finding (sell-side M&A advisor, Discretion Capital):** Buyers want confidence you'll be around 3-5 years. Moats = confidence = multiples. No moats = distressed.

### For Founders (Even Bootstrapped)

Even if you never sell, these moats are defensive mechanisms against the 10 attacks.

---

## Evaluation Framework: 8 Questions for Your Business

One question per moat. Answer each honestly:

1. **Moat 1 (Trust):** Who's built their career or business around recommending or defending you?
2. **Moat 2 (System of Record):** Do you hold the definitive view of the work? Are you the system of record or just a view?
3. **Moat 3 (Action):** Do you take action or just recommend it?
4. **Moat 4 (Trust output):** Do customers trust your output enough that they don't check you?
5. **Moat 5 (Approvals):** What approvals, regulations, or legal stuff do you hold that a newcomer has to wait for?
6. **Moat 6 (Network):** Who has to agree to replace you? One person or everyone at once?
7. **Moat 7 (Learning):** Does one customer's experience make it better for everyone?
8. **Moat 8 (Burden):** What do you maintain that you resent maintaining?

---

## Paths to Build Each Moat

If you don't have a moat, where can you move?

1. **→ Trust:** Build an ecosystem. Become the recommended vendor. Cultivate partners.
2. **→ System of Record:** Take a point solution and make it central to operations.
3. **→ Action:** Move from reporting to actually moving money/taking action.
4. **→ Trust Output:** Build accuracy, track record, regulatory confidence.
5. **→ Approvals:** Become an approved/certified provider in your regulated industry.
6. **→ Network:** Move from single-seat to organization-wide coordination.
7. **→ Learning:** Collect data from all customers, feed improvements back to all.
8. **→ Burden:** Embrace infrastructure/DevOps burden that others avoid.

---

## Bottom Line

**If you have 1-2 of these moats, you're probably doing well.**

**If you have 0, you're vulnerable to the 10 attacks and commoditization.**

**Priority:** Figure out which moats are yours or which ones you can move into. Lock in defensibility.

**Outcome:** Defensible business, higher valuation, survivable in AI-disrupted market.
